MR. WINCH-LOSS OF PERSONNEL AND PLANE DURING NAVAL EXERCISE
speechtext:
rise on a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, and it is a matter of regret that I have to do so. Approximately nine months ago 22 members of the defence committee of the House of Commons were privileged to join naval exercises taking place between Halifax and Bermuda. A part of the observation of those exercises was made on board an Argus aircraft. From the 10th to the 20th of this month, for the first time in parliamentary history, four members of the House of Commons were invited to be observers at what is known as the Canada-United States "Springboard" naval exercise off Puerto Rico. It was an exhilarating experience. Part of the exercise, sir, included an a.s.w. search by an Argus airplane.
We returned, sir, at nine o'clock last Saturday, that is the four of us who represented all hon. members here. It was therefore with a great deal of shock that this morning we learned that an Argus aircraft participating in the "Springboard" exercise which we just left had disappeared with 16 Canadian servicemen on board. I feel it is only right that I, as one who has just returned from that exercise, should rise on a point of privilege to pinpoint this fact, that during war we expect casualties. We maintain the armed services in time of peace for the defence of our country and, if called upon by a vote of the House of Commons, for the maintenance of peace throughout the world.
This tragedy hits me very hard, just having come back from Puerto Rico and the "Springboard" exercise, and I want to direct attention to what we sometimes forget, that is, that our men and women in our armed services, even while we are not at war, and especially those aboard ships and a.s.w. aircraft, risk their lives every day, as has been demonstrated by what happened during the past few hours to one of our Argus aircraft, at a time just five days before the warships in the area were to return to their home base at Halifax.

Question of Privilege
I know, sir, you will understand my rising on this point of privilege, as one of the four members of the House of Commons attending that exercise, to express our sympathy to the relatives and friends of the 16 who died in this regrettable catastrophe in the service of Canada, and to pinpoint that lives of service personnel are being risked on behalf of this country and on behalf of the peace of the world in both war and peace.

subtopic: MR. WINCH-LOSS OF PERSONNEL AND PLANE DURING NAVAL EXERCISE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the plane came from my constituency and since there were personal friends of mine on that plane, I had intended at the proper time to ask for a statement with respect to the accident. Perhaps the minister is now prepared to give such a statement, explaining what happened and possibly giving a list of those on board.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: MR. WINCH-LOSS OF PERSONNEL AND PLANE DURING NAVAL EXERCISE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and that of the house I will do so. I regret that I have to confirm the news reports of the crash of an Argus aircraft of R.C.A.F. maritime air command, involving a serious loss of life.
The aircraft, from No. 404 squadron based at Greenwood, Nova Scotia, was participating in a joint Canada-United States exercise off Puerto Rico, and was reported to have crashed into the sea some 60 miles north of that island at 10.50 eastern standard time last night. The report was made by the Alcide, a British submarine attached to the Royal Canadian Navy and taking part in the exercise. Immediate action was taken to institute a search of the area and three R.C.N. destroyer escorts, H.M.C.S. Annapolis, Gatineau and Terra Nova, were orderd to the scene.
I am sorry that I have to inform the house that the latest messages received indicate that there were no survivors. A full inquiry in an effort to determine the cause of the accident is being undertaken immediately.
The aircraft carried a crew of 15 R.C.A.F. officers and men. In addition, a defence research board scientist from the naval research establishment at Bedford, Nova Scotia, was on board. I am sure all hon. members will join me in expressing to the relatives and friends of those who lost their lives our sincere regrets on their tragic loss.
I cannot let the occasion pass without paying tribute to the outstanding work of the officers and men of the maritime air command. Highly skilled and dedicated to their

work, they have maintained in all types of weather, over the years, constant anti-submarine patrols at very low levels over the waters off our shores both in the Atlantic and Pacific.
Due to the calibre of the men and the level of their training, maritime air command has achieved a record of efficiency and flight safety that is second to none. Indicative of this is the fact that prior to last night the Argus aircraft, which came into service in 1958, had not been involved in any major accident or loss of life while flying a total of more than 132,000 hours.
While our sympathy goes out to relatives and friends, the loss of such men is not only theirs but that of Canada as a nation.

Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing):

Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays-from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., from 2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m. and from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m.; Wednesdays-from 2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m. and from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m.; provided that proceedings on an adjournment motion, if any, on Mondays, Tuesdays or Thursdays shall be taken up at 11 p.m. on any of the said days; and

Business of the House
I had hoped that it would not be necessary to move it. I will be perfectly frank and say that I do not like longer hours any better than anybody else. However, I do think we have got into a situation where we have created in our rules structure the right of veto on the part of any individual member at the end of any day's sitting to prevent any extension of the sittings for a few minutes or for an hour after ten o'clock at night. This veto exists even though it may be obvious that the consensus of all those but one in the house at that moment, is to continue and finish the particular item before the house at the time.
That right of veto has crept into the rules. It is a comparatively new one and, I must say, has created some real difficulties in getting business determined by the house. This is accompanied by the fact that the evening sittings are only two hours in length rather than three hours as was formerly the case. I think those who will be celebrating an anniversary the day after tomorrow will well remember and share with me the opinion that the last hour between ten o'clock and eleven o'clock at night seemed to be a rather effective time to get a good many debates finished up.

If the house sat the number of hours provided for in this motion it would be damaging to the work of hon. members and the staff, and in the long run would produce the kind of atmosphere in this house which would not be conducive to the passage of legislation. In fact we wonder how long it may take to debate this motion.
We would like to suggest to the government house leader that he let this motion stand and ask the house to agree to extending the hours of sitting on the three nights that we now sit-Monday, Tuesday and Thursday- until eleven o'clock instead of ten o'clock. We recognize that these two hour evening sittings provide a vehicle for getting nothing

done, but perhaps with an extra hour we might be assisted in putting some of the remaining legislation through.
We understand the arguments put forward by the house leader, but suggest that we could put forward arguments on the other side of the case. This house should seriously consider how best to complete this session in a responsible and agreeable fashion. This party offers this suggestion quite straightforwardly that instead of adopting this motion the house leader ask for consent of the house to immediately extend the hours of sitting on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays until eleven o'clock. We are opposed to morning sittings and to the addition of sittings on Wednesday and Friday nights. We agree to the provision in respect of matters under provisional standing order 39A.
The motion as a whole is, I think, unacceptable to the house. I could move an amendment to it, but I do not think that is necessary. I urge the government house leader to consider the alternative proposal we have put forward.

Business of the House connection. However, the question I have in mind is, do extended hours ever contribute to the conclusion of a session or the expedition of the house business? It seems to me that all this does is provide an opportunity for extended and expanded debate.

Mr. Speaker, like the other house leaders of opposition parties I feel that the motion brought forward today by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) should have been considered a little earlier. This motion appeared on the order paper last Friday and since then the government house leader has not called the other party leaders together in an attempt to agree on the hours of sitting.
Monday, Tuesday and even this morning, the President of the Privy Council would have had the opportunity to call together, in accordance with the usual rules and procedure, the leaders of the various parties in an attempt to reach an agreement. But he rises now, without a word to anybody and moves the adoption of this motion about which we had not heard anything before it appeared on the order paper.
It can be seen that all the members of the opposition seem to object to this motion. The business of the house is being delayed by stands and tactics such as those of the house leader at this time. Why attempt to impose the idea of one group upon the other groups? Had there been consultations, an understanding might have been reached; but on the other hand, if he maintains his attitude it is possible that this day will be lost again and that by six o'clock we still will be talking about the extension of the sitting hours.
Therefore, following the hon. members from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and

Business of the House Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I suggest to the house leader, the President of the Privy Council, that he should withdraw his motion, discuss it with the house leaders of the other parties and submit it again, so that this afternoon we may resume our debate on the pension plan. I am convinced that we will have reached an agreement by then. Otherwise, I can assure the President of the Privy Council that he will waste the whole afternoon of the house, because we are not willing to accept such sitting hours.
In the first place, the staff of the House of Commons, who have worked long hours do not deserve being treated thus. Indeed, the President of the Privy Council mentioned a while ago that this session had already lasted 241 days.
Second, I object to legislation being passed under pressure, in haste, as the leader of the house would like to. Many days have already been lost because the government could not arrange its work in an orderly fashion. Today, after having received the advice and the views of this side of the house, I believe that the President of the Privy Council should postpone this motion until tomorrow morning, enter into discussions this afternoon or tomorrow morning. I am convinced that it will be possible to reach an agreement and to soon end this session.
On the other hand, if the government tries to impose such hours I am afraid that it will be losing its time more than it has done previously. Imposing such sitting hours would be a bad example to set.
That is my suggestion, and I hope that the President of the Privy Council will take it into serious consideration. He should have consulted with the leaders, but he did not do so. He can still do it this afternoon and tomorrow. Instead of wasting the time of the house, why would he not let his motion stand until tomorrow and in the meantime call a meeting and discuss the advisability of saving the time of the house.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the indulgence of the house to make a statement in connection with Professor Sibley not having been admitted to Canada on Friday last. My officials brought this matter to my attention late Thursday afternoon, just before I left Ottawa for the west coast. The department had learned of Professor Sibley's proposed visit through the newspapers. There had been no request to the department, as is customary in some such cases, for his admission to give lectures in Canada.
The information received by the department indicated that he was a person whose admissibility to Canada was open to question under the terms of section 5, subsections (1) and (m) of the Immigration Act. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read those portions of the act. Section 5 begins in this way:
No person-
I will skip the next few words.
-shall be admitted to Canada if he is a member of any of the following classes of persons:
(1) persons who are or have been, at any time before or after the commencement of this act, members of or associated with any organization, group or body of any kind concerning which there are reasonable grounds for believing that it promotes or advocates or at the time of such membership or association promoted or advocated subversion by force or other means of democratic government, institutions or processes, as they are understood in Canada-

The last few words of that paragraph are not necessary in this context. Then paragraph (m) reads:
(m) persons who have engaged in or advocated or concerning whom there are reasonable grounds for believing they are likely to engage in or advocate subversion by force or other means of democratic government, institutions or processes, as they are understood in Canada;
Now, Mr. Speaker, section 20 of the act is the one which guides the actions of examining officers. It provides:
Every person, including Canadian citizens and persons with Canadian domicile, seeking to come into Canada shall first appear before an immigration officer at a port of entry or at such other place as may be designated by an immigration officer in charge, for examination as to whether he is or is not admissible to Canada or is a person who may come into Canada as of right.
Every person shall answer truthfully all questions put to him by an immigration officer at an examination and his failure to do so shall be reported by the immigration officer to a special inquiry officer and shall, in itself, be sufficient ground for deportation where so ordered by the special inquiry officer.
I am not going to read section 23, but I would like to refer to sections 23 and 24, which deal with what happens when the special inquiry officer comes into the act. In section 27 there is a proviso for a private inquiry with the opportunity for providing counsel.
In reading and in referring to those sections I am not saying that they are as they should be, as to how the law should be. That is a matter for parliament to decide, and I am sure hon. members of the house were as pleased as I was when some time ago the Prime Minister announced the government's intention to prepare a white paper and to open up the Immigration Act for revision at the next session of parliament. Personally I feel so strongly about the necessity of amendments to the act that I doubt if I would have been minister today had it not been the government's intention to recommend before the end of this year that the act be amended.
But, Mr. Speaker, pending changes in this act, as I see it, my duty and that of my officials is to administer the act as it is to be found on the statute books at this time. In fulfilling this duty I want to make it clear that I made no decision that Professor Sibley could or could not be admitted under the act. According to Hansard, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition alleged that I had made an order refusing admission. That, Mr. Speaker, is incorrect. I shared, whether rightly or wrongly, the considered view of senior officials of my department that on material reported to me there was a doubt as to

whether Professor Sibley was admissible, at least admissible until we had further information.
The legislation of this parliament instructs officials what they are to do if there is such a doubt. That legislation is perfectly clear. This course was explained to Professor Sibley when he arrived in Canada on Friday. Since there was some doubt, it had to be resolved by a special inquiry.
At the request of the Prime Minister I have checked the facts carefully on the spot in Winnipeg. Professor Sibley was properly questioned under section 20 of the act. He was questioned by a competent officer and he was told he could not be admitted without a special inquiry, that is, an inquiry giving the right to counsel and to cross-examine witnesses.
Neither the examining officer nor I were prejudging or had prejudged the results of any such inquiry. The doubt that the examining officer was expressing was a genuine one. It was a legal doubt under the legislation that we are charged with administering. In recognizing this doubt we were simply following the law; we were passing no judgment on Professor Sibley's character, sincerity, scholarship or other qualifications or qualities.
If the department went outside the law at all, it was to perform an act of courtesy. The superintendent of immigration in Winnipeg on Thursday informed the Voice of Women organization in Winnipeg that there was some doubt as to Professor Sibley's admission. I am advised that this information was conveyed to Professor Sibley in Minnesota during the evening of Thursday last. I should add that the departmental officials in Ottawa at no time had any definite advance information as to when and how Professor Sibley was planning to arrive or whether, in view of the information given to the Voice of Women on Thursday, he would in fact make the journey for the date in question.
This was the position reported to the Prime Minister when he inquired of the department at lunch time on Friday. It was at 2.45 p.m. Ottawa time that my officials, having in the meantime received a report from Winnipeg, told the Prime Minister's office that Professor Sibley had in fact arrived by plane at about 1.20 p.m., Ottawa time, and had chosen to leave again rather than be subjected to the special inquiry, which could not have been properly conducted until early the following week. I would say that I was so advised while in Vancouver, and also immediately teleimmigration Policy
phoned the Prime Minister's office. It was then about three o'clock, and I could not get the Prime Minister because he was in the house, but I spoke to one of his senior staff.
This information, however, was not available and could not have been made available to the Prime Minister at 2.30 when he answered a question according to the information which had been made available at lunch time. It seemed to me then, and still does seem to me, that in recognizing the doubt as to Professor Sibley's admissibility, based on reliable information before me, I was following the course which the law laid down for me to follow. However, in this matter we should not be and are not concerned only with the administration of immigration law. We should be and are concerned also with the rights of Canadian citizens, specifically their right to the free exchange of ideas. This was also canvassed when I was in Winnipeg.
Some Canadian organizations had invited Professor Sibley to Winnipeg. They wanted to hear him, and I regret because of the circumstances that this right was interfered with.
Professor Sibley arrived in Winnipeg only shortly before he was due to speak-a matter of a few hours-consequently the doubt as to his admissibility, which legally we had to recognize, could not be resolved in time to enable him to keep the speaking engagements. This meant-and it is unfortunate that this is so, but this is the case-that the choice the law allowed us to offer Mr. Sibley was academic from his point of view. The inquiry could not be held before he was due to speak. He therefore preferred to leave again rather than to wait and have the doubt about his admissibility resolved.
I might say, however, that Professor Sibley intends to return to Canada. That arrangement was made before I arrived in Winnipeg. He will return in the very near future at a date to be agreed upon. Those arrangements were made and discussed I think during his recent visit. He is to appear at such a special inquiry and he will have counsel because he is entitled to counsel. I might say that I have met and spoken with the counsel. He is a respected and able member of the Canadian bar.
There is a genuine conflict between the rights of Canadians to listen to what ideas they choose, and the rights and procedures regarding immigration as defined by the statute.
However, Mr. Speaker, it is my view that our Immigration Act ought to recognize the difference between people who apply for

Immigration Policy
admission to Canada as landed immigrants and those who come here on the invitation of Canadians to give lectures or make speeches. However, the act makes no such distinction, and in revising it later this year parliament might be wise to consider such a change. I intend to suggest it in the white paper that is being prepared.
Perhaps the suggestion might be implemented by incorporating a provision in the act that, if anyone arriving at a border point can show he intends only a short term visit for a speaking engagement, or some similar purpose, sponsored by a reputable Canadian organization, such as a university or the Voice of Women, then such a person should be allowed to proceed, even if there be a doubt as to his admissibility for any long or protracted period. In other words, for a short term visit of this kind the legislation would make it clear that we do not have to try to resolve the questions that would be asked if a man or woman were applying to be a landed immigrant, or were planning an extended visit, which would afford time for a full inquiry. In this way for the short term visitor the rights of Canadians, that is their rights to listen to whom they wish, would be put ahead of normal immigration requirements.
The only way such a change can be made as a general procedure is by amendment to the law. In the meantime, I intend to do what I properly can within my existing legal authority to follow an administrative course which will reduce to an absolute minimum the danger of conflict with considerations of free speech and the rights which are involved not only for visitors but also of Canadians who choose to listen to lecturers from outside Canada.
As a new minister in the immigration department I should like to end by saying that the responsibilities that parliament and the legislation in its present form have given to the minister and his officials are difficult and, most of the time, delicate ones. I honestly do not believe that any human being can discharge these duties in accordance with that existing law and procedure without making some mistakes. I hope I am not going to make any, but if I do I also hope you will bear with me. In the short time that I have been with the department, and, I might say, contrary to views that I have often heard expressed in this house and elsewhere, I have already learned that on the whole the department of immigration's standards of conscientiousness and efficiency are high. I am

surprised and pleased, in view of the frequently unwarranted attacks which have been made upon it, to find that the morale and the efficiency of the department are very high; and as I have said I am pleased with this fact. I and my officials will do our best to make the amendments which, in my view, unquestionably are needed.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the house might appreciate this incident. During the course of my visit to Winnipeg-I had a busy schedule, starting at about 6.30 p.m. and continuing until 12.30 noon the next day-I saw many people, but the most human thing that I saw was a group of 100 or so students on my arrival at the airport, carrying banners. When I went out to meet them later they still carried the same banners. I explained that I could not make a statement until I had completed my investigation and had made a statement in this house. But I was very amused not only with the kind reception that they gave me but with some of the signs they carried. One said "Welcome, Mr. Nicholson. How did you get in?" Another one said "Rivard is free, why not Sibley?". It was a typical college youth demonstration done with sincerity and with good humour, and it did lighten my few hours in Winnipeg.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has the faculty of being able to present a bad case in a rather happy way. He has endeavoured by touches of humour to laugh off a situation serious in its import and dangerous to freedom in this nation. When the minister raises the excuse that what he has done has simply been done under the statute, may I ask this: How did Rockwell, the nazi leader from the United States, get into Canada on two occasions? How was it possible for him to come? For after all that took place under the present administration, the explanation given by the minister cannot be accepted as a just and proper explanation of the very serious matter at stake in this case.
All I know is what I read in the papers. But when the minister speaks of the reception he got from the students, I think it appeared in the papers and was broadcast over the radio that he also had a bodyguard of police to protect him.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I did not have any bodyguard. I walked from the plane to the immigration

office, just about the same distance I am now from the Leader of the Opposition.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Even when one has
guards, one can be as close as that without being in any danger.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: The minister said he had no guards.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Let me say immediately that this explanation is one that cannot be accepted. I do not know anything about Professor Sibley. However, I do know that the vice president of the United States, Mr. Hubert Humphrey, according to a telegram which I have received from the Voice of Women, has stated that the federal government of the United States will take any steps necessary to investigate the incident. He also added that he had known Professor Sibley personally and he termed him a respected scholar. The president of the University of Minnesota, Meredith Wilson, has said of Sibley that he is a man of good character and highly regarded among political scientists in the United States. His point of view on nonviolence in the United States is a legitimate part of the present debate on international policy.
The minister says that no harm has been done to Mr. Sibley. Well, I do not know how you can smear a person more with McCarthy-ism than by what has been done in this case; let that be perfectly clear. I may disagree with what Mr. Sibley would want to say. But the explanations given in this house indicate a serious dereliction of duty on the part of the department of immigration. They indicate that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was not told the full facts. They indicate that an official in Winnipeg, Mr. Cross, had advised the Voice of Women, I think it was on Thursday last, that this man's reputation was such that it might be difficult to permit his entry into the country.
A question was asked of the Prime Minister in this house on March 22 by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), as reported at page 12634 of Hansard. It is as follows:
Is it the policy of the government to force organizations that wish to invite a speaker here for one day to get a clearance from the government before that person is allowed in?
The Prime Minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker; but there are occasions when this is desirable, in the light of the information which government officials have in respect of the man in question who is being invited or in connection with the organization which is inviting him.
Immigration Policy
The organization which was inviting him was the Voice of Women.
This is one of those matters which is not administrative. It is not a question of administrative lawlessness. Action was taken. I am told that the minister confirmed the order that was made in Winnipeg.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR

Mr. Speaker, I must necessarily accept the denial; but what, then, was the minister doing when the matter was brought to his attention? What did he do-in face of the smearing of a man who sought to make a speech before a respectable organization regarding matters of international importance? I am told that on Thursday evening at 6.45 Dr. Lockhart of the United College in Winnipeg was in touch with Mr. Cross of the department of immigration and was advised that Mr. Sibley was not to be permitted to enter the country. Mr. Cross was asked why that was so, and he answered: "I cannot tell you, but it was an order from Ottawa". I ask, who gave the order? What did Mr. Cross mean when he said that the reason this man was going to be denied entry into Canada was because of an order from Ottawa?
I am told by the representative for the Voice of Women that when Mr. Sibley arrived at the airport the procedure was as follows. He was informed that he would be held in custody until a hearing was set up. In other words, he would be held in custody until this week, for the minister has admitted that the hearing would not take place until Monday or Tuesday. Or the alternative was that he could go back.

Order. I realize the important principle involved in this discussion. But it is not up to the Chair to decide the substance of this matter; I have to apply the standing orders as given to the Chair. May I recall to all hon. members-this seems to be the right moment to mention this-that with regard to the business of the house standing order 15, subsection (2a), which is a new subsection in this session, says:
On motions, as listed in section (2) of this standing order, a minister of the crown may make an announcement or a statement of government policy. subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, no one is trying harder than I am in that regard.

But the minister went out of his way to exculpate himself and his department; he went out of the way to explain the limitations on freedom. Surely on a matter as important as the liberty of the subject he will not interfere with a discussion in this regard; for this indeed is a shocking case, a shocking example of bureaucracy at its worst, whether it was confirmed or not.
Keeping within the limitations that you have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, I want to review what has taken place in this matter. It is an alarming and it is an inexplicable situation that has been created. Now they say to Mr. Sibley, "You are out. We would not let you speak. But if you come back we will treat you differently". It is like calling Rivard back.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
They are now saying to Mr. Sibley, "Come back; please come back, and we have decided that we are going to give you different treatment". This is after they have maligned him in a way that will

cause him to suffer for the rest of his life. The minister himself in Winnipeg-again I am speaking from the information I have-made this statement to the Voice of Women, "If you knew what I know I hope you would have agreed with the action taken". If all that the minister knows is what he told the house, the action taken is totally inexcusable; and let that be clear. He said to the Voice of Women, "If you knew what I know". What does the minister know? Did this man come over here for the purpose of stirring up revolution, for arousing the Voice of Women to become a combative organization? Is that why he came here? The government wanted to preserve this peaceful group of women from the influence of this terrible man who would arouse them to become bellicose.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: What manner of nonsense is this? Is the government trying to establish a kind of arid conformity in this country? The minister gave a lengthy explanation and I want to refer to that. I took down what he said. He was concerned about the freedom of the mind. The way in which the minister is going to meet this problem is to have a white paper.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: A whitewash.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
We do not want a white paper; we want some reason for the application of the law as it now is, because in my opinion this is the first time anything like that has occurred in this country. Are we going to destroy freedom within Canada? A man coming into Canada has no right to do wrong. Freedom is the right to be wrong, not to do wrong. Yet this man is judged by some officials, and the minister said he did not approve. All I have to say is that the information I have is to the effect that he did. The minister says this is not so, so we are going to ask for the production of the documents in this connection.
Are ideas to be policed? This is the government that has tried to apply thought control in political matters in Canada. Are they going to try now to apply thought control in the thinking of Canadians? This, Mr. Speaker, is wrong. What the minister should have done today was rise in his place and state, "I am sorry that this happened". But instead of doing this, he stubbornly gets up and continues to besmirch Mr. Sibley's reputation by inference and innuendo and says, "Well, if he comes back we will give him another

chance to prove that he is not what we know him to be".
I was under the impression-and I know something about the Immigration Act-that orders such as this have to be confirmed by the minister. I refer to orders such as were made by Mr. Cross in Winnipeg. If that order was not confirmed, then I believe it is in fact a nullity. Sir, imagine in 1965 a government that believes that unorthodox minorities shall be penalized. It does not seem to realize that unorthodox minorities often become orthodox majorities. What this government deserves in this connection is a stern rebuke from this House of Commons.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: Now the minister says, "Well, after all I had my officials, and my officials are excellent people". That is no answer. Justice often dies in the hands of those that are excellent people unless there is somebody to speak out on behalf of those being treated unjustly. Abraham Lincoln once said, "To serve by silence when they should protest makes cowards of men". We protest, and protest most strongly what has happened in this connection. I come back to this point, Mr. Speaker. This matter rests on the shoulders of this government and it cannot be shelved by generalities of the kind that we have had presented. The minister said today, "I shared the considered views of my department". What does that mean? Those were his words. Does that not mean that he approved of what they did; that he approved of this conduct that is so-well, I am restricting my language, but I must say that this type of thing has given Canada a black eye in the United States.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: I rise again, Mr. Speaker-

I shared-the considered view-of my department-

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR

Mr. Speaker, the minister is now finding himself in a difficult position. Those are his words and I simply repeated them to show they place the responsibility right on the back of the government. The minister has said that he shared the considered view of his department. What was the considered view, that this man was dangerous?
What has happened here has given Canada a black eye in the United States and in any freedom-loving country in the world. This is action which cannot be justified in any way, and no kind of fantastic explanation or verbiage can remove the condemnation that is his. The government can in no way take action to remove this condemnation.
The minister has been continually jumping up and down. Will he say that he felt, following his examination of the facts, that Sibley was going to raise a revolution or bring about a change; that he was going to take the Voice of Women organization and transmute them into fighters for a revolution and change the government of this nation by force? The explanation he has given is so ridiculous that one can only say it is in fact an alibi for action in respect of which there should have been an apology made to parliament rather than a disposition which still leaves a smear of McCarthyism.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement seems to indicate that this government, which has not been successful in keeping undesirable characters in Canada, has been overzealous in keeping some very desirable people out. The minister seems to be under the impression that by simply making a categorical statement without any corroboration he is advancing an argument.

Immigration Policy
The minister concluded his remarks by saying that he had tremendous confidence in the staff of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I point out to you that in his remarks he admitted that the decision to question Professor Sibley was taken on Thursday, yet the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) did not know this on Friday afternoon at two thirty o'clock despite the fact that he had consulted with department of immigration officials between 1 p.m. and 2.30 p.m. that afternoon. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister had received a telegram, as he said to the house yesterday, in the morning from the Voice of Women organization. After consulting with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration officials during the lunch hour he then stood up in this house, as recorded at page 12575 of Hansard and said:

subtopic: WINNIPEG-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
I respect the remarks of the minister, but if the officials at Winnipeg, who had apparently received instructions on how to deal with this man the day before, had been fulfilling their duty they would have telephoned the department here in Ottawa to inform them when Professor Sibley was arriving.
As I was saying, at that time we discussed whether someone should take the lead in going to the airport in order to provide Professor Sibley with the legal counsel to which he was entitled. As a result of that discussion Professor Gibson left the university and went to the airport with that intention in mind. He was unable to reach Professor Sibley, who had arrived at approximately 12.20 in the afternoon, and therefore submitted to an immigration officer a letter addressed to Professor Sibley offering him legal counsel.
Immigration Policy
After Professor Sibley had been questioned and had chosen to go back to Minneapolis rather than spend the week end in custody awaiting the setting up of an official board of inquiry, the same immigration officer was asked whether the message had been delivered to Professor Sibley. The reply was, as has been recorded in the press, "He did not ask for it". It seems to me that someone has goofed in this matter.
I am concerned about this, because it is my particular privilege to cross the border to the United States often on speaking engagements. Never to this day have I been questioned, other than is normal when you pass by the immigration desk, nor have I ever heard that it was necessary for a person from the United States coming to Canada for the purpose to have a request submitted to the immigration service of Canada.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think it would have been much better in this particular instance if the minister, for whom I have great respect, had merely said that perhaps they were too hasty, that this was an error on their part. This professor holds a very responsible position in a very respectable university, and it was an error to treat him the way he was treated. It seems to me that reasonable Canadians agree that even if Sibley may have been regarded as an extremist in many ways he should not have been denied entry because it was expected, perhaps, that he would express views in contradiction of the policies of the state department of his country and, as we have found within the last few days, contrary to the policies of our own Department of External Affairs.
This is no excuse for barring him entry to this country. I know the members of this house know my own stand in regard to that particular issue which involves Viet Nam. On the other hand, I do not see how we can be justified in barring a citizen of the United States, who obviously had no intention of subverting or overthrowing the government of this country, from entry to this country. I believe in the light of all this it would only be proper to apologize to Professor Sibley for the way he was treated, and the debate should be closed on that note. It seems to me that the department made a very poor decision.
There is a point I should like to make that has not been mentioned by the minister or by any of those who have spoken before me, which I feel is extremely important. It involves the security of this country. All we have to do is look back over the last few

Immigration Policy
weeks to realize that there have been a number of Canadians involved in some form of subversive activities. I am concerned about this, and as I travel about the country I find a lot of other people are also concerned.
As I mentioned only a few days ago in the house, it is imperative that the government do something about laying down some sort of policy relating to the security of our nation. I mention this now because obviously someone in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration had a fear regarding the advisability of letting this man come up and lecture on the topic on which it was expected he would lecture.
I ask this simple question. Had the F.B.I. given any notice to the department, or to those responsible for security in Canada, about this man Professor Sibley? I know the department must have been aware well in advance of the type of man he was. I say that because the Voice of Women-though I do not understand the reason this organization circulated the document I am making reference to-openly stated in that document that this man was going to deliver a lecture on peace as it related to United States government policy at this time.
This document also stated that he was a controversial man who had advocated setting up campus clubs espousing communism, the violent overthrow of governments, free love, nudist colonies and other controversial subjects. Assuming that the department must have had access to this type of information, did it contact the F.B.I. with regard to this man? Was there a proper investigation made, or not? If there was the fear, which apparently there was, that led to the decision that he be stopped at the border, or that a special court of inquiry be set up, it seems to me it should have been the department's responsibility and the far wiser course to inquire from the other side as to the status of this man relating to security.
I do not intend to speak much longer on this, but I do urge it as being very important to the government that a situation such as that which occurred last Friday should not be allowed to occur again. Either a white paper should be prepared, outlining just what is the situation in Canada so far as security is concerned, or we should adopt a policy similar to that in the United States where the F.B.I. has full responsibility for security, and from time to time publishes documents giving necessary security information to the public.
[Mr. Thompson.)
It is not good enough to continue as we are doing now. Whether we like to admit it or not we are facing a very serious situation in the world today, and the security of this nation is of basic importance to its future and the well-being of its people. It seems to me the government could well avoid an incident like this, a very unfortunate incident, if it would only firm up some policy and put it into action.
Again I say this whole incident was most unfortunate. The very thing that apparently the officials who made the decision had intended to prevent has now been amplified 100 times over. Publicity which arose out of this action has been far worse than that which would have attended a single lecture to the Voice of Women organization in Winnipeg, a lecture that might have received a little publicity in the local press and might or might not have been reported across the nation. However, the issue that is involved is much bigger than this one incident. Not only does it involve the right of freedom of speech and the freedom of expression, but it involves the security of our nation and its future well-being.

speechtext:
1.	Has any estimate been made of the number of office workers and clerical staff in the automobile industry and the automobile parts industry who will be out of work directly or indirectly as a result of the Canada-United States automobile agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CLERICAL STAFF AFFECTED BY CANADA-U.S. AUTOMOBILE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
1. The program for the automotive industry is designed to achieve a substantial expansion in production and employment in Canada. It is, of course, not possible to predict where these increases will take place but we hope and expect that it will take place in all segments of the industry. The matter of how the expanded labour force in the industry will be distributed between various categories of workers including office workers will vary from company to company depending on how these companies adapt themselves to the new opportunities for expanded production and greater specialization. We have no evidence to suggest that for the auto and auto parts industry taken as a whole there will be a net reduction in office and clerical staff.
2. There are retraining programs operating on a continuous basis in most cities and towns in which motor vehicle or automotive parts manufacturers are located. These programs are designed to give the best type of retraining available to the worker, depending upon his skills and his interests. This service is sufficiently flexible to offer appropriate retraining to office workers or clerical personnel.

Mr. Chairman, last night I concluded my remarks by quoting the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), who said that we are justified in fearing an increasing interference of the state in the private and economic life of a nation, which would reduce the initiative of the peoples and of the citizens.
When I consider the accumulated funds which will be made available to the government I also agree with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) who in 1963 also expressed her fears about those accumulated funds in the hands of the government, which might eventually be accumulated in such a way as to become dangerous for the interests of the human person or of individuals or of private enterprise. She expressed that fear on several occasions. I am one of those who also share her fears. The plan we are now discussing, Bill No. C-136, is not merely a new factor, it is the result of a new pattern of political thought which the various parties in this house have been developing for a few years.
I remember that in 1962-63, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare feared the setting up of those pension funds, this accumulation of funds, we in Quebec precisely heard those famous slogans: "Masters

in our own house", "The key to liberation." We also spoke of a policy of greatness, of the responsibility resting on the leaders of the state of Quebec, and at the same time, to say that one is a leftist was becoming more and more the thing to do. We had some from the far left in provincial politics and even in the provincial administration. Others, perhaps not of the extreme right-have definitely shown their lack of confidence in private enterprise and in the respect due the individual in order to counteract at that time, I believe, the trend of the political, economical and social life in the province of Quebec.
But a lot has happened since 1962, since the introduction of the first pension plan in the house, in 1963. There are still some leftists in the province of Quebec; there are those who were leftists but who are less convinced now; there are also those who, today, claim to be left of centre, as Mr. Jean Lesage stated. Some claim to be rightists, but not of the extreme right, like Mr. Emilien La-france, Quebec family and welfare minister, and many other ministers. Therefore, the Quebec legislators are divided as far as political thinking is concerned.
After consideration of the motions for first and second readings of Bill No. C-136 and its reference to an all-party committee, it seems that all those who were called upon to scrutinize this piece of legislation have already been convinced of this political attitude: The state must increasingly grow in importance and huge capital must increasingly be made available to the state.
But, I said and I repeat that what was true yesterday is also true today. In support of my apprehensions and of the apprehensions of some of my fellow citizens of the province of Quebec in respect of these pension plans, either under Bill No. C-136 or under the bill to be passed by the Quebec legislature within 30 days after the passing of Bill No. C-136 and which seem to centre more and more around compulsory mobilization of savings, I will quote a few excerpts from an article published in the newspaper Le Front Ouvrier on December 17, 1949, under the heading:
Are we on the road to slavery?
Dealing specifically with the major social security aspects of pension plans, the article had this to say:
We have a question for the industrialists, the capitalists and the present masters of the economy. We shall not beat around the bush. Bluntly, here it is:
Is the logical and irrevocable end of the capitalist system the reintroduction of labour slavery
Canada Pension Plan
under the domination of the state representing capitalists only? Is that the goal of our capitalists? What steps will they take to prevent our falling into servitude?
Naturally, we shall wait for their reply but it is action we want at this stage.
At that time, the then minister of labour, Mr. Mitchell, had just said:
In Canada, it is the government which will set up a pension scheme for the workers.
Does industry share this opinion? Will it allow the state to head for socialization because it would rather have the workers reduced to slavery by the state instead of having them participate in management?
And let not industry, no more than Hon. Mr. Mitchell, suggest that social security cannot be provided by private enterprise because its permanence is not guaranteed. Our readers will find in opposite columns a practical means (there are also others) to ensure the workers' security without subjecting them to the state and without half the cost of this social insurance being used to pay handsomely a whole army of officials, who will not produce anything and who will finally live off the labour of the workers.
The purpose of Bill No. C-136, or of the bill which the Quebec legislature intends to pass within 30 days after the passage of this bill, is to establish in this country a state capitalism under which many bureaucrats, inspectors, auditors and even policemen will confiscate pay books in private enterprise. Are we not establishing such a system?
Yesterday at the beginning of my remarks I said that after a long and difficult period of gestation we were about to attend the birth of a democratic monster, and I believe that is the direction we are giving the economy of our country.
I also said that this problem was important and far reaching since it was stated that Bill No. C-136 was the most important social security measure, and it is, after all, compulsory contributory social insurance.
I will now quote views that I endorse.
The pension fund is not a cure-all, either with regard to social security or with regard to the independent economic growth of a nation. The universal pension fund Mr. Lesage is talking about is not a make-believe paradise able like a drug to solve by magic all problems.
It is a way to organize the economy and social security.
With regard to that method, I deplore the fact that the committee which studied that bill did not take into account the large volume of evidence supplied by experts in economic, actuarial and investment matters.
I realize that some may think that I am defending the insurance companies here, because on February 15, 1965, the finance minister had this to say:

Canada Pension Plan
The national pension plan, said he, is probably the most important social security measure ever introduced in this country. The principle of this bill was unanimously approved last fall and a joint committee considered it thoroughly.
Certain circles which have been strongly opposed to it in the past two years have suddenly changed their opinion and said they would support the bill if certain major amendments were made.
Further on, he said:
It would be disastrous if the national pension plan was not adopted at this stage because of lobbying by organizations which have been against it from the start.
I admit that in the beginning opposition was mainly voiced by those who had a good knowledge of actuarial practices, economic consequences, administration of private pension plans. And that is probably the start of the opposition to this concentration of power which, as I said, is dangerous in the hands of the state, because this accumulation of funds will be used as at present and, for all practical purposes, it is only a financial instrument in the hands of governments.
We are told that insurance companies were the only lobbying organizations. I will quote here from a brief submitted by the executive board of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. Not only representatives of insurance companies were involved; there were also representatives of industry and business, people who speak for the public and practically all the classes of society. Here is what they said about this cumulative fund on page 11, paragraph 5 of their brief:
Consideration should be given to the effects of the establishment of an important retirement fund on the capital available for the productive sector of the economy.
The following dangers are to be feared following the setting up of a national plan:
1.	The compulsory contribution of savings will put investment capital at the disposal of the government, and the latter will not have to rely on the regular money markets for its financial needs.
This means that the Quebec government must, within 30 days of the passage of Bill No. C-136, pass a law to that effect, and instead of going to the American brokers to borrow the necessary capital, instead of going to the usual money market, it will be able to use these very funds.
Hon. Gerin-Lajoie stated on July 3, 1963, as reported in La Presse:
There are reports that the minister of youth, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, is already considering the establishment of a school credit office which would draw its funds from Mr. Lesage's pension fund. This office would make loans or would, in turn, allow the school boards to borrow from the fund

for school construction purposes, at "conditions of reimbursement within their means".
And we know that three quarters of the school boards in the province of Quebec were, until recently, showing perennial deficits, because the increase of the compulsory tax forced the government of the province of Quebec to deny them any grants. They had to revise generally the rates of school taxes in the province of Quebec.

I believe I can easily relate the pension plan to what I said when I dealt with the use of funds which will be accumulated under this bill. When reference was made to the Quebec bill, we often heard the following words: comparable, adaptable, parallel, identical. Moreover, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare is willing to recognize the fact, we are going to pass a measure considered and worked out by the socialists for the left wingers of the province of Quebec. I believe that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will admit that this bill will bear economic after effects as regards the province of Quebec. When this fund will be channelled through the pension plan, the Quebec plan, which will have to be comparable with Bill No. C-136, will have the same repercussions.
On this matter, I will also quote other excerpts from the memorandum submitted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, paragraph 2, page 11:
2.	The sources of private capital would decrease, and there would result therefrom a transfer of financial duties from the private to the public sector.
Under this bill, $6 to $7 billion of capital will be drained off during the next 20 years, and also between $4 and $5 billion in compulsory savings under the retirement fund of the province of Quebec.
This means that from $10 to $11 billion will be drained off and handed over to various departments at various administrative levels, or to crown agencies. In other words, as I said a while ago, out of those accumulated

funds, the province of Quebec will be able to build bridges and roads, and the accumulated funds under the provisions of Bill No. C-136 will also be used by the other provinces.

Mr. Chairman, the nine other provinces will also be able, under Bill No. C-136, to use part of the 45 per cent which can be accumulated by the governments of those nine other provinces that will come under this proposed legislation.
Here are a few more fears expressed by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce:
3.	The investment decisions left in the hands of government agents will undoubtedly come under political pressures unrelated to economic requirements.
To stay within the limits of Bill C-136, how do we know that the government of New Brunswick, through an authorized agent or corporation, will not use part of those funds for such and such a project, while this Bill No. C-136 is being presented to us today as a vast program of social security?
How do we know that social security will not be increasingly resorted to in order to accumulate funds? How do we know that the capital saved will not prevent private enterprise from making investments that not only would enable it to survive but would prevent it from being completely crushed by a dictatorial regime such as the Minister of National Health and Welfare feared in July 1963?
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce goes on to say:
The capitalization of a fund on the scale contemplated under a plan of national scope would be a form of compulsory savings established by the state, the effects of which will be felt more heavily by those people with the lowest income.
Mr. Chairman, I think that is has been proved on several occasions that it is precisely 20220-8074
Canada Pension Plan
those who do not earn enough who lack the bare minimum. In fact, according to a statement by the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), it was found that there is extreme poverty in the rural areas of the country and some figures were even given showing that 200,000 or 300,000 families lack the necessities of life, because their income is below standards considered as a vital minimum.
After earning their first $600 in salary these people will have to contribute a part of their income as savings for the accumulation of a state fund under Bill No. C-136 or under the measure which the province of Quebec proposes to pass. In fact, those funds will be used to set up a slave system under state capitalism. And I continue to quote the complaints expressed by the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce:
The setting up of a reserve fund without any accounting relation between the amount collected and the benefits paid would create a capital reserve without any special affectation which would be assailed from all sides by multiple requests.
The increased expenses, resulting from the implementing of the projected plan, will exert a pressure which will weaken our competitive position on the domestic as well as on the foreign markets. The contributions will certainly raise the prices of goods and services involving a high percentage of manpower.
Mr. Chairman, I will give a single example only of the possible consequences in certain areas of the Canadian industry.
In the pulp and paper industry, or in the lumber industry in Canada, where 50 percent of the companies' over-all expenses represent labour wages, the consequences will certainly be more serious than in the case of companies engaged in finance, wholesale, trade etc., because in industries where automation is increasing, the salaries represent a dwindling percentage of the over-all expenses. Consequently, some sectors of the Canadian industry will feel it more.
Mr. Chairman, I have the impression that some will say that the arguments coming from this side of the house must not be taken seriously. However, to support my views I will quote the words of an expert in economic matters who is certainly well known in Canada at the present time. They come from a speech delivered by Mr. William Hood, professor of economics, recently appointed adviser to the Bank of Canada, before the members of the Canadian political science association and the Canadian association of law professors. I quote:
The transfer of capital from the private to the public sector will slow down the accumulation

Canada Pension Plan
of capital reserves in the private sector. I am worried because a decrease in savings in the private sector will slow down the massive accumulation of private capital and will therefore endanger that sector's ability to undertake vast projects essential to the development of productivity.
Mr. Chairman, these are the remarks I wanted to make at this stage of the business of the house, considering the funds that are going to be built up after this Bill No. C-136 has been passed. I hope that those who have not already done so, will take the time to read the committee proceedings and the various briefs that have been presented. They will find some serious warnings concerning the repercussions that will be felt throughout Canada in the economic, political and social fields.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Health and Welfare is shaking her head, meaning that there will not be any serious repercussions. In this regard, I would suggest that she look up the committee reports of proceedings, where she will find that the deputy ministers of finance have expressed the opinion they could not say for sure what will be the consequences of the compulsory monopolizing of the low wage earner's savings under Bill No. C-136.
In my opinion, there will be serious consequences and I still maintain that we are now working up a method of directing the economic and social life of the Canadian people.
I ask my colleagues who could not attend the committee meetings during the recess, to read the proceedings on the various briefs submitted and especially to look into them fully. They will realize then that it is not so urgent to pass Bill No. C-136.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, up to this point I have not spoken about the Canada pension plan. In fact, there has been little opportunity to discuss its over-all implications because under the new procedure arrangement we have bypassed statements at the resolution stage and on the first clause until after the clauses have been studied in detail, and after the committee has done its work. I agree that this is one of the most far reaching pieces of legislation we have had before parliament for a very long time,
[Mr. Perron.)
and therefore it is something that certainly ought to be considered from every aspect. Perhaps there never has been more complex legislation before this parliament. At this time I am concerned about the over-all impact of this act as we have come to understand its intricacies. Likewise I am concerned about the developing resentment which I find across the country as the public have a better opportunity to understand what it really means to them.
At the outset, I would say there is a place in Canada for a contributory pension plan that is completely portable under which Canadians could invest their savings, and apart from any universal welfare plan. It has been a very unfortunate situation in so far as the wage earners in Canada are concerned that there has not been portability of past or present pension plans. As a result there has been a great injustice worked upon our working people. If there could have been such a portability arrangement, the justification for this plan would not be present.
It is a rather tragic state of affairs, however, that the Canada pension plan has been tied to the over-all welfare structure. It now relates to old age assistance, veterans and disability pensions, widows' pensions and so on. In view of this fact, this legislation has become unnecessarily complex. I believe the people of Canada are going to resent what this bill holds in store for them. I am convinced it is certainly not going to be to the political advantage of the Liberal party because I believe people are going to feel the whole thing has been misrepresented to them, once they understand what returns there will be for them.
When I say this, I am convinced that up to this time the general public have not realized what this plan means. This is true also of most of the members in the house, especially before they had an opportunity of studying it in the special committee. In other words, in my opinion, all that would have been necessary would have been a contributory savings plan. Again I say that if private pension plans had been portable, this plan would not have been necessary at all. I say that the old age pension, war disability, widows and other types of pensions should have been left separate, except for the lowering of the minimum age to 65, and making provision to bring pensions up to a point more compatible with the cost of living. Perhaps the strongest argument for this lies in the fact that so many Canadians are com-

pletely omitted from this Canada pension plan. Also this plan is absolutely unfair to the self-employed. Certainly, the compulsory features of the plan are not acceptable to many when applied to such an item as pensions.
In fact the self-employed will get a rude shock when they see what they are in for. I agree with other speakers who have said that it will amount to nothing more than another income tax. In fact it is a regressive tax, taxing most heavily those who can least afford it.
Some very useful information has been published by various newspapers across the country, and I wish to refer to one of a series of articles carried by the Winnipeg Tribune of recent date, particularly in reference to the topic I have mentioned, that the pension plan would be much more satisfactory if it had not related to old age security or welfare in general. This article says:
It is apparent that no large body of opinion today opposes the principle that everybody in old age should receive adequate financial benefits. At present the two main sources for this security stem from private investment and the old age security program. The first, unfortunately, doesn't cover everyone, and the second is inadequate. C.P.P. is an attempt to marry them in a shotgun wedding. ..
After ten years only one third of Canada's retirement age people will be receiving C.P.P. benefits averaging $45 a month, and there will be 1.2 million receiving only O.A.S. After 20 years there will be perhaps a million without C.P.P. benefits at all. In the far distant future C.P.P. on its present basis will exclude almost half of the retired population from any worth-while benefits. As a social measure it is totally inadequate. A further extension of O.A.S. would be far more equitable for the retired Canadian, and encouragement for extension of private plans, such as in Ontario, would be more rewarding to all wage earners.
This is a very significant fact. For example, a young person who is 20 years of age and is self-employed, will pay $8,100 by the time he is 65. In addition to that there will be a much larger sum of accumulated interest- that is, if he earns enough net income in order to pay the maximum contribution to the Canada pension plan. At 65 he begins to draw benefit, and if he lives until 70, drawing something over $100 a month, he will draw a total of $6,120. Even if he lives only a few years longer than present day normal expectancy of life in Canada, he will never have a chance to draw the total of his contributions, and certainly not that which should be rightfully his in accumulated interest.
Canada Pension Plan
I am the first to admit that this plan will be of great benefit to myself and to others in my age grouping who are able to pay the maximum contributions. Anyone with $5,000 a year net earnings will contribute $1,350 over 15 years as a wage earner, and it will take him only 13 months to get that money back. Thus it is a good deal for practically all members in this chamber. Those of us who are past 40 years will receive much more than we actually contribute, even though we only live to the normal life expectancy.
But I am thinking about our children and those young people who are in their twenties. It is a very poor investment for them. We will skim the cream off the milk that the younger generation will have to provide. This is one of the great inequities in the plan, and the government and the minister cannot get away from that fact.
Again I refer briefly to the editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune of March 20 under the heading, "Short Changing the Young":
Every high wage earner over 45 stands to gain something out of C.P.P. Those over 45 in the $5,000 wage bracket will receive pensions of 500 to 1,000 per cent on their premium investment. They are the fortunate drones but after them the benefits will be watered down, so that when the time comes for today's young bees to retire the pattern will be completely reversed and they will be confronted with percentage losses of even greater magnitude than the drones profits.
A young worker bee of 20 today making annual investments of $158.40 (the same as C.P.P.) in a joint program with his employer could get $2,370 in his annual pension on a private annuity-rated plan. He will get only $1,250 from C.P.P.
This represents one of the great inadequacies of the plan and is something we should all be concerned about. If this is a fact, and I am convinced it is, then we are deceiving the people of Canada by telling them this is for their benefit. I am concerned about some of the statements which the minister made with regard to the plan because I think they completely misrepresented the plan as formulated.
On July 18, 1963 the minister said that "the purpose of the government's proposed legislation was to ensure that as soon as possible, in a fair and practical way, all Canadians would be able to retire in security and with dignity." That will not be the case and has never been a possibility in connection with this plan, because the plan does not cover all Canadians. In fact it covers best those who need it least, and it leaves a sizeable proportion, something like 30 per cent, who will receive no benefits because they will not be eligible.

Canada Pension Plan
On September 9, 1963, again talking about the Canada pension plan, the minister said "its purpose was to make it possible for all Canadians to retire in security and with dignity." This plan does not do that, and to tie it in with welfare is completely confusing the issue. It may have its value as a contributory savings plan. However, I doubt that, because it gives a poor financial return. But certainly as a welfare measure it is completely inadequate, and to say it will provide all that is necessary for retirement in security is absolutely wrong. By saying that, we are presenting it to the Canadian people as something which it is not.
It is a compulsory, contributory savings plan, nothing more and nothing less. As such it has some value because it offers complete portability, something we have not been able to obtain by any other means. But as a welfare measure it is a tragedy that it has been presented to the Canadian people as an adequate pension provision.
I support the government in its decision to lower to 65 the minimum age requirements for old age assistance. That was good, but it did not go far enough. Since 1958 we in the Social Credit party have advocated that if we are to make pensions in any way commensurate with the cost of living, old age assistance should be $100 a month. At that time, and it was only seven years ago, this was away out on the fringe of things and we were laughed at.
Yet at this time it is something that the majority of members agree is a necessity. It is no longer branded as unrealistic, fanatical, nonsensical; it is something which we agree today is necessary.
Therefore I would have thought that the government would have brought in a program along with the lowering of the minimum age requirement, a similar program working in reverse order, where each year until 1970 they would have increased the benefits of the Old Age Assistance Act so that by that time the pension would be $100 a month.
I realize that we do not get money from some secret source. This type of money must be supplied by the taxpayer-contributor. It would have been a very realistic approach to a problem that I believe all of us in this house agree is a necessity to meet, namely, to increase next year old age pensions from $75 to $80, the year after that from $80 to $85, so that by the time we reach January 1, 1971, it would give every senior citizen over 65 $100 a month. This would have taken care of our old age welfare in a respectable and

legitimate way. This has not been done. Actually, what has been done is to confuse the welfare picture with a contributory savings plan, and I regret this very much. However, that is the fact of the matter.
If I may refer briefly to the over-all welfare picture, it is customary for Canadians, particularly Canada's politicians, to regard Canada's welfare expenditure as below that of other countries. If you would permit me, Mr. Chairman, as this matter is involved with the Canada pension plan, I should like to bring out the point that this is not the case. Canada today is contributing a larger proportion of its national income to welfare than most countries in the world. It is often said in this house and on the public platform that Sweden is an example to be held up as the way welfare responsibility is adequately met. On the other hand, I find that Sweden does not spend nearly as much of her national income on welfare and health as does Canada. In this regard I refer to all forms of welfare, including pensions, family allowances, hospitals and medicare, unemployment insurance and any other cost transfer made from government to individuals and householders.
