speechtext: Do not forget the veterans.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
In August of last year the Financial Post carried some interesting statistics. For example, Japan spends 5.2 per cent of its total net income on welfare. The United States spends 6.9 per cent, Australia 7.9 per cent, Britain 8.1 per cent, Denmark 9 per cent, Sweden 9.9 per cent. However, in 1963 Canada spent 11.6 per cent; and in this past year, 1963-64, Canada spent 12.5 per cent of her net national income on welfare. Only two major countries in the world spend more than this: West Germany, with about 15 per cent; and France, with approximately 16 per cent. I am not saying that in face of the statistics we are meeting our responsibilities as far as legitimate welfare is concerned in this country, but I am indicating that we are spending a sizeable amount of money on welfare out of our total national income. But we confuse the picture if we add into this a compulsory contributory savings plan such as the one we are talking about.
My concern in all of this is that we are committing ourselves to welfare programs that are distorting the true priority picture as it should be, and at the same time we are tying a weight of taxation around our necks- because this is where this money must come from under our present system-which will be difficult to bear. In fact, I think it is es-

sential that we put welfare in its proper priority.
As far as I am concerned as a parent, I believe the number one priority in welfare refers to the education of my children. I believe that the number two priority refers to the health and care of my children and my dependants. The number three priority is that we find provision for the future, and provision for those who are unable to take care of themselves, as the next logical priority. 1 think most Canadians will agree with me on this. But by committing ourselves to the type of welfare program that this is, we are placing our priorities in reverse order, and because of this I am concerned whether we are going to be able to meet the other necessary elements of welfare when they come before us.
I was reading the other day a brief from the Canadian school trustees association which was submitted to the royal commission on taxation, where it states, in terms of constant dollars education costs will rise from $1.7 billion in 1961 to $3.3 billion in 1971 and $4.4 billion in 1975. Then I read in the Hall commission report that as far as a national health plan is concerned it is estimated that within ten years we will be spending a minimum of $10 billion on a national health program, should it be instituted, and the cost will more likely be nearly $12 billion. Combine this with the fact that we will be spending in this pension plan a total amount of money estimated to be $7 billion to $8 billion in the next ten years. Add all this together and we find an obligation ahead of us, as far as welfare is concerned, which is going to be double that which it is now.
I believe that because we are being forced into a program such as this, as we have at the present time, we will be in serious difficulty in Canada in meeting what I believe is our first priority, that of adequate education and educational facilities; and second, those obligations which relate to the general health and welfare of the nation. Therefore I regard this legislation in this respect as a very dangerous piece of legislation-first because it deceives us as to what it actually is, and second, because it commits us to something which is going to be far more costly, yes and far less profitable, than we are anticipating.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would again ask your indulgence to make a few remarks which relate to the over-all pension plan as it comes into this field of welfare. I have to mention the welfare program because this
Canada Pension Plan
Canada pension plan does relate to welfare, even though I think it would have been far more advisable if it had not. I would suggest to the minister that one of her first obligations to this house, and also to the Canadian people as far as health and welfare is concerned, is that she should take three or four important steps to avoid our getting further into the situation into which we are rapidly being propelled by this pension plan, assuming that it is going to pass-because I think that at this time the majority of the members of this house are in favour of it.
The first step is that areas of priority must be laid down whereby the most urgent welfare needs are met first. The need for priorities has been emphasized by many different sources. I think it is necessary for us to spell out over the next ten years what are the legitimate areas of welfare, and their urgency. Second, I think complex problems such as costs-we have heard a great deal said about the cost of this pension plan- must be laid before us for what they represent in order that we can understand how these priorities will be met. Third, I think there must be provision made for adequate integration of the private pension plans which we have at the present time, with a view to integrating them into the Canada pension plan, and at the same time providing portability for these plans so that we do not lose the investment that is represented in them. Then fourth, it is essential that we project the long range cost of welfare so that we can fit these priorities into what will be a legitimate share of the net national earnings of our people, which will be devoted to the general welfare program that we regard as essential, particularly recognizing that we have a greater area of responsibility today in this field than we have ever had before.
If the government had done this before, I am convinced we would never be in the position that we are in the house at this time, namely on the verge of accepting a plan that does not actually represent what it has been purported to be. It is confusing the welfare situation. We will not be taking care of our senior citizens, nor those unable to provide for themselves, in an adequate way. We would never have found ourselves at the point of almost being forced to accept something that within ourselves we know is not right; and I am sure many members on the government side feel this way about it as well.
I will not continue my remarks further at this time, Mr. Chairman, but I believed it

Canada Pension Plan
was essential to again emphasize some of the facts relating to this plan which may or may not have been brought out in the debate, which has already been a very long one. I hesitate to think that the government or any member of this house who plans to support this bill can go out and represent it for what it has been said it is supposed to be. Let us regard it as a compulsory-I do not like the word "compulsory"; I think it is wrong-contributory savings plan that has a worth-while benefit because it is portable. But let us not confuse it with welfare. I have been disturbed as we have gone over the various clauses of the bill to find that the means by which this plan can be altered and changed are so difficult, because I am convinced the plan is soon going to have to be changed because of its complexity and difficulty. In my view we are simply locking around our neck a plan which before too long I think we are going to wish we could change.
So I would say to the members of the government and also to the members of the opposition, many of whom have dealt with different aspects of the plan and have drawn attention to its inadequacies, that we owe it not only to our children-I do not think we owe it to ourselves, because we will come out all right-but to those people who are expecting something better out of the plan than they are going to get, to make very clear what it actually is and not be guilty of misrepresenting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might ask a question of the hon. member before he resumes his seat. I wonder whether my hon. friend has had an opportunity to look at the proceedings before the committee, and particularly at page 706, where he will find that he is in error in the quotations he has given with respect to social security expenditures in other countries as percentages of gross national product in 1960. If he has not, may I suggest that he look at page 706, where he will find that the expenditure in Sweden, which he said was less than in Canada, was in fact 12.4 per cent, in the United Kingdom it was 11 per cent, and in Canada 8.9 per cent.
May I also, before resuming my seat, advise my hon. friend that the Financial Post figures which were quoted by him-I am sure it was not his intention to give incorrect figures- included health expenditures in this country, a fact which was pointed out by myself in a letter to the editor of the Financial Post,

which was acknowledged with thanks. My hon. friend may not know that, but I know he would not want to mislead the committee with regard to the figures he has been using.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not been misleading the committee in any way at all, because the figures I quoted did not refer to the gross national product; they referred to the net national earnings of this country, which is a far different thing than the gross national product. The gross national product is a very fictitious thing because it includes a great many things that have no relation to the net national earnings of the Canadian people.
Furthermore, I did not misrepresent the figures that were quoted from the Financial Post, because I was speaking of the over-all cost of welfare in Canada and not as it relates just to the federal government. I was very careful to state that I was referring to all forms of welfare where government money was actually paid out to individuals or households, or for the benefit of individuals or households. I believe these statistics are absolutely correct in this regard. I was emphasizing these statistics to show that in the over-all picture, under the federal system which we operate in Canada we are spending more on welfare than most of the major countries in the world; and those statistics are absolutely correct.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question. I noticed his reference to the term "net national income" in regard to the statistics he used. I wonder whether the hon. member would indicate to the committee the source of the statistics he used, or were they his own calculations based upon statistics he obtained?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The statistics are not my own calculations, Mr. Chairman. I do not have the exact title of the document that I used, but it was an official report which, by the way, I obtained from the Department of National Health and Welfare. They included the over-all statistics concerning welfare at the municipal, provincial and federal levels. Most of the statistics, as far as the national picture is concerned, were taken from that document. If the hon. member would like the title of the document, it is in my office but I do not know the exact title at the moment. I think it was published in 1958. I have also taken some of the statistics contained in the recent report with regard to the first annual survey of the economic coun-

cil of Canada; and I have taken a few of the minor statistics from the bureau of statistics and some private statistical organization. In no case did I use my own calculations.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: May I ask a further question, Mr. Chairman. What was the source of the statistics with reference to the other countries to which the hon. member referred?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I quoted from the Financial Post of August, 1964. While these figures, as the minister has indicated, were not just for the federal picture, they related to the over-all picture including health, because health and hospital insurance programs must be included in this particular calculation if you are going to arrive at the over-all picture. It is unfair to compare it with Sweden as a national government and Canada as a national government, because we have allocated, under the British North America Act, which is our constitution, that health, education and other forms of indigent welfare are the responsibility of provincial and local government. Therefore, to give an over-all, national picture you must include governments at the different
Business of the House levels in order to assess what we are spending on welfare as it relates to the national income of the country and the Canadian people.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must remind you that it is now six o'clock.

Progress reported.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I could have the indulgence of the house for a moment I would like to say that the house leaders had a meeting this afternoon and agreed that tomorrow, Thursday, the house would not rise at ten o'clock in the evening but would sit for an extra hour until eleven o'clock. I would ask the unanimous consent of the house in so ordering.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the house give unanimous consent?
Agreed.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
